newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel calls for world health reform.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel calls for world health reform.

text.p: A leading medical ethics centre on Monday called for changes in treating the world's health problems with a shift away from a technical emphasis on cures toward preventing disease and caring for the sick.

The panel's report, issued by the Hastings Centre in Briarcliff Manor, New York, also advised developing nations to avoid the path of developed nations that have created inequitable health-care systems "whose hallmarks are expensive and elaborate technologies and high costs."
An emphasis on new technologies to cure disease and prolong life causes a host of problems, the panel of experts from 14 nations said.

"Longer lives have often come at the price of greater suffering and higher costs, both to the individual and society," the panel wrote. "Technological advances often increase inequity and are increasingly difficult to finance."

The panel called for an emphasis on preventing disease and injury and promoting good health, noting, for example, that a community-wide anti-smoking campaign is more valuable than "heart transplants for comparatively few citizens."

It also called for an emphasis on pain relief and care for the terminally ill, saying that in its view not all illnesses can be cured. "Care of the dying should be seen as having the same importance as care of those who will go on living, despite the common unwillingness of modern medicine to admit defeat," it wrote.

The panel included physicians and medical experts from Germany, Hungary, Great Britain, the Slovak Republic, Spain, Chile, Italy, Sweden, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Indonesia, the Netherlands, China and the United States.
The Hastings Centre publishes journals on medical ethics and conducts research on ethical and medical issues.
